finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures, revised on a second pass. Shops usually sell a coolant service at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor, so the built totals are a floor-to-middle view. They are for a plain drain and refill with the maker's coolant; a machine exchange or a chemical flush costs more. Built totals (coolant + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2022 Honda Civic 2.0L about $122-$285 (2 gallons of premix for a 1.56 gal change); midsize 2016 Toyota Camry 2.5L about $126-$297 (2 gallons for a 7.7 qt system); truck 2016 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 5.3L about $160-$359 (5 gallons of premix for a 16.6 qt system; that is the whole system, and a simple drain and refill uses less, so the truck's real coolant cost often sits nearer the low figure); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $113-$268 (1 gallon of concentrate for a 7-7.6 liter system; the BMW comes out lowest only because concentrate goes twice as far, and its bleeding procedure tends to push labor to the upper end). Against the benchmarks: the car totals cover Jerry's drain-and-fill figure ($80-$150), Jerry's average ($173-$184), Kelley Blue Book ($131-$209) and Capital One's chain-shop range ($175-$250). FIXD's $98-$123 is at or below our floor and looks like labor only. YourMechanic ($301-$337) falls inside the truck range and just above the car tops; RepairPal ($440-$512) is above everything here, and its parts figure of about $285 is far more than coolant costs ($23-$119 here), so it likely covers more than fluid. A fair plain-language range is roughly $120-$300 for a car and $160-$360 for a full-size truck, more for a machine flush. What changed on this pass: the truck class is now filled, using a Silverado 1500 because GM's manual capacity and GM's own list price for Dex-Cool loaded while the Ford capacity table and a Motorcraft list price did not; the economy and midsize capacities now come from the makers' own manuals, which meant changing the examples to a Honda Civic (Honda's online manual) and a Toyota Camry (Toyota Canada's manual), with the same Honda and Toyota coolant prices as before. Caveats, stated plainly: the Honda manual page does not print the model year (2022 by its publication code); the Toyota manual pages read do not print the model name or year (it is identified by its two engines); the Silverado manual read is the later Silverado LD edition (copyright 2018) of the same truck and engine; the BMW capacity is still from a reference table, not a BMW document, and the BMW high figure is a retailer price for genuine coolant, not a list price; the two Aisin low prices are multiplied on the assumption that each is a one-gallon jug, which the pages do not print. How solid the hours are: the labor time is one general statement of 45-90 minutes from a guide co-written by two mechanics, backed by a 30-60 minute do-it-yourself guide; neither is vehicle-specific or a flat-rate book time. No Honda, Toyota, GM or BMW stated time for a coolant replacement was found: the manufacturer documents that turned up either bundle the coolant work into a larger repair, tell the dealer to use clock time (GM bulletin 25-NA-052), or cover something else (Hyundai 1.1 hr for a hybrid battery coolant loop; Karma 3.0 hr for a low-volume luxury car). No national chain menu price could be loaded. Posted menu prices loaded on 2026-11-20 from eight sellers' own pages (one regional chain, five dealers and two independents in California, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Kentucky, Texas and Connecticut) run from a 'starting at' $93.99 to $269.95 for the whole car, mostly before tax and shop fees, with the dealers at $149.95-$269.95; two of the eight are chemical-cleaner flushes, not a plain drain and refill, and no national chain page that loaded printed a price. Reviewer note: one dealer menu (Columbus, OH: $164.95 brake fluid, $189.95 coolant) was dropped from the posted prices because its page was last modified in 2021. Five more posted prices were added later on 2026-11-20, all from dealers' own pages in Louisiana, Texas, Colorado, Washington and New Jersey: $149.95, a $179.95 coupon, a $232.43 coupon for a drain, pressure test and refill with up to one gallon, $253.95 for a service worded as a flush and $269.95 for a service named 'Drain and Fill', which keeps the dealer prices inside the $149.95-$269.95 already seen.
extras: A quote often adds a coolant disposal or environmental fee, shop supplies and sales tax. A machine exchange or chemical flush, a cooling system pressure test, a new radiator cap or a thermostat are common add-ons. Leaking hoses, a seeping water pump or a clogged heater core found during the service are quoted separately. Vehicles with separate cooling loops (hybrids, turbo intercooler circuits) or a vacuum-fill bleeding procedure take longer. Trucks and large engines need more coolant than the car figures here.
